questions.text: Consider two decision problems Q1,Q2 such that Q1 reduces in polynomial time to 3-SAT and 3-SAT reduces in polynomial time to Q2. Then which one of the following is consistent with the above statement?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Q1 [latex]\le_p[/latex] 3-SAT, and 3-SAT is in NP [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q1 is in NP.
- 3-SAT [latex]\le_p[/latex] Q2, and 3-SAT is NP-hard [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q2 is NP-hard.

Answer: Q1 is in NP, Q2 is NP hard

options: Q1 is in NP, Q2 is NP hard.
Q2 is in NP, Q1 is NP hard
Both Q1 and Q2 are in NP .
Both Q1 and Q2 are NP hard

questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Lexical analysis: DFA minimization (2)
- Parsing: production (parse) tree (4)
- Register allocation: graph coloring (1)
- Expression evaluation: post-order traversal (3)

Answer: P-2, Q-4, R-1, S-3

questions.text: In the context of abstract-syntax-tree (AST) and control-flow-graph (CFG), which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Option 1: in a CFG a loop edge goes back to earlier code [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] false.
- Option 2: CFGs have cycles for loops [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] false.
- Option 3: an AST node can have as many children as the construct needs, and a CFG node (e.g. switch) as many successors as the code has [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] True.
- Option 4: a CFG basic block can contain many statements [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] false.

Answer: The maximum number of successors depends on the input program

For any input program, neither AST nor CFG will contain a cycle
The maximum number of successors of a node in an AST and a CFG depends on the input program

questions.text: Consider the basic COCOMO model where E is the effort applied in person-months, D is the development time in chronological months, KLOC is the estimated number of delivered lines of code (in thousands) and [latex]a_{b},b_{b},c_{b},d_{b}[/latex] have their usual meanings. The basic COCOMO equations are of the form
questions.solution:
Basic COCOMO: effort from size, then time from effort.

[latex]E=a_b(KLOC)^{b_b},\quad D=c_b(E)^{d_b}[/latex]

Answer: E = [latex]a_b[/latex](KLOC)exp([latex]b_b[/latex]), D = [latex]c_b[/latex](E)exp([latex]d_b[/latex])

questions.text: A system has 6 identical resources and N processes competing for them. Each process can request atmost 2 resources. Which one of the following values of N could lead to a deadlock?
questions.solution:
Deadlock is possible when every process holds one less than its maximum and nothing is left: N [latex]\times[/latex] (2 [latex]-[/latex] 1) [latex]\ge[/latex] 6, i.e. [latex]N\ge6[/latex].

Strictly, none of 1, 2, 3, 4 can deadlock (with N = 4, after each holds 1 there are still 2 free). The question is flawed; the official key marks N = 4, the largest choice.

Answer: 4 (as per key)
